title: US Envoys Shuttle Between Kyiv and Moscow in Push for Peace
summary:
In a high-stakes diplomatic shuffle, top US envoys met with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday, just a day after sitting down with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. The visits mark the first time Donald Trump's envoys have traveled to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion began.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the US negotiators, said they felt "encouraged" after what they called a "substantive" discussion with Zelensky. Kushner said President Trump had instructed them to find a way to end the war and "create the right conditions for a long-term, durable peace."

But the path to peace is riddled with thorny issues. Zelensky insisted that any deal must include security guarantees for Ukraine and a "dignified" post-war peace. "We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer," he wrote on social media. "Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed."

The envoys' trip was not without drama. They flew to Poland, then took a train to Kyiv because, as Zelensky explained, it wasn't possible for their plane to land. While in Kyiv, they met at St Sophia Cathedral, near where a Russian drone had hit the headquarters of Ukraine's security services just days earlier.

In a rare gesture, Putin and Zelensky agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days during the envoys' visit. That's a small but symbolic step toward de-escalation.

However, the war rages on. Ukraine's military said it struck an oil refinery, an airfield, and two air defense systems in Russia. Meanwhile, Russia launched 108 long-range drones and small cruise missiles at Ukraine, according to Ukraine's Air Force. Ukrainian defenses shot down 82 drones and six missiles, but 11 locations were hit.

Witkoff praised Zelensky's "unsurpassed" hospitality and said the US team would continue negotiations "as long as it takes." The Kremlin described Saturday's talks with Putin as "frank" and "constructive."

As the envoys head home, the world watches to see if these talks can translate into a lasting peace. For now, both sides remain entrenched, but at least they're talking.
why_it_matters: If these negotiations fail, the war will keep shaking Europe's security, energy supplies, and global alliances; if they succeed, it will show that even entrenched conflicts can move toward talks. For young people, the story is a window into how diplomacy—not just military force—shapes the world they are inheriting.

background_read: Ukraine has been fighting a full-scale Russian invasion, and this round of US shuttle diplomacy is an attempt to find an off-ramp.
U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and then Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv within the same weekend.

Zelensky, Ukraine's president since 2019, says any deal must contain security guarantees because earlier promises have not protected his country; Putin, Russia's president for more than two decades, is trying to keep the upper hand.
St Sophia Cathedral, the venue in Kyiv, is one of Ukraine's oldest and most symbolic churches, while the nearby drone strike showed how close the war remains.
Past cease-fire diplomacy has often stalled over enforcement, so the three-day pause on capital strikes is best read as a first test, not a settlement.

perspectives.description: The envoys describe their talks as substantive, and the three-day pause on strikes on capitals is a rare sign of mutual restraint. When leaders keep talking, there is at least a chance of building toward larger concessions.

The same days show how distant peace remains: Ukraine says it hit Russian military targets, and Russia launched 108 drones and cruise missiles at Ukraine, with 11 locations hit. A short pause that covers only capitals does not protect people elsewhere, and the core security guarantees Zelensky wants are still unresolved.

Shuttle diplomacy between capitals often produces cautious optimism before the hardest bargaining begins. The article notes that both sides remain entrenched, so the symbolic pause is a first step rather than a framework for peace.

The key test is whether the US team can turn encouraging words into a written plan that Russia accepts and Ukraine trusts. Will security guarantees be strong enough for Zelensky, and will Putin accept a deal that does not look like a victory?
